claims.claim: By the best cell counts we have, a typical man is about half human.
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8):e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533; full text PMC4991899 (Europe PMC fullTextXML, fetched 2026-11-18) + Hatton et al. 2023, PNAS 120(39):e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120; full text PMC10523466 (Europe PMC fullTextXML, fetched 2026-11-18)
claims.note: Sender: 'We estimate the total number of bacteria in the 70 kg "reference man" to be 3.8·10^13 ... revise past estimates to 3.0·10^13 human cells'; 30/68 = 44% human. Hatton: '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg); 36/(36+38) = 49%. Sender's B/H '1.3, with an uncertainty of 25%' spans ~38-51% human, and Sender calls it 'about 1:1'. 'Typical' is Sender's own word: 'the typical adult human body consists of about 30 trillion human cells and about 38 trillion bacteria'. 'By ... cell counts' fixes the measure as count, not mass. 'Best' is evaluative framing: these are the two most recent whole-body counts; Hatton: earlier studies 'converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells'. Not true for every man (Sender Table 3 'elder' 22 vs 38 = 37%), which is why 'typical' and the on-screen 'typical 70 kg man' matter.

claims.claim: Hook at second two (A4): the viewer has heard 'By the best cell counts we have,' ('have,' 1.670 s; 'a' 1.962 s; 'typical' 2.176 s; 'half' 3.367 s). Look 1 shows 68 unlabelled neutral dots in a human outline; Look 2 shows the unsplit Vitruvian Man with 'BY CELL COUNT' (from 'cell' - 4 frames until 'about').
claims.source_checked: src/generated/cell-count.alignment.json (75 words, identical to the script's spoken text); src/shorts/cell-count/index.tsx (first Tag from F.half; bacteria dots dim from 'about'); src/shorts/cell-count-cutout/index.tsx (card 1: 'BY CELL COUNT' at F.cell-4 until F.less-1; split/tissue/'ABOUT HALF' from 'about'/'half')
claims.note: At 2.0 s no claim has been made and nothing on screen implies one; the popular false form (10:1, '90% bacteria') is never said or shown. A viewer who stays to ~4 s gets 'a typical man is about half human' with 'typical 70 kg man' on screen in both looks, which both papers support (44-49%). Confirmed; framing. Side note: the alignment json's own sha256 field (2178aa34...) is not the script's sha; its word list matches the current script exactly.

claims.claim: Entry 4: total bacterial mass ~0.2 kg; a bacterium is on average far smaller than a human cell; Sender revises earlier statements of 1-3 kg (1-3% of body mass), citing an NIH news release (its ref. 25)
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8):e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533; full text PMC4991899 (Europe PMC fullTextXML, fetched 2026-11-18)

claims.note: The numbers are right (Sender 3.0e13, 2.5e13 RBC, 3.8e13). The labelling statement is not true of Look 1: its human total is shown three times as a label, and only the first ('30 TRILLION' / 'typical 70 kg man (2016 count)') carries the tag; 'HIS 30 TRILLION' / 'counted, not weighed' and the closing chart's '30 TRILLION' / 'his own, mostly blood' do not (Look 2's '30 TRILLION (2016)' on card 9 does). Fix, either: (a) add '(2016 count)' to the sub of Look 1's closing '30 TRILLION' label (and ideally 'HIS 30 TRILLION'), e.g. 'his own, mostly blood (2016)'; or (b) reword SOURCES entry 8 to 'labelled "(2016 count)" where the human total is first shown, and on the cutout's comparison card'. (a) is preferable since the closing card is the chart's payoff and Hatton's 36 differs.
